title: Architects of Prairie Avenue
premise: An autumn afternoon with the architects who reconstructed Chicago: Jenney, Richardson, Cobb and Frost, Burnham and Root, Beman and Hunt, concluding where Burnham encountered his future wife.

opening.text:
JAUNT: ARCHITECTS. An autumn afternoon on Prairie Avenue, 1904, the declining sun raking across masonry. Thirty-three years ago Chicago burned; it reconstructed itself as an audacious modern metropolis, and numerous architects responsible for that reconstruction designed residences along this avenue, for clients whose resources were effectively unlimited.

Seven residences on foot, from 1701 to 2100 Prairie: the engineer who constructed the first skyscraper, a colossus from Boston, the partnership of Cobb and Frost, the youthful Burnham and Root, the designer of an entire company town, the architect of the Statue of Liberty's pedestal, and the commission that launched Daniel Burnham's career. He married his client's daughter.

Commence at 1701, with a restrained Italianate façade by a profoundly unrestrained engineer.

stops.text: 1701 Prairie, William G. Hibbard's residence of 1869, commissioned by the president of a substantial wholesale hardware enterprise. Its architect, William Le Baron Jenney, trained as an engineer, and fifteen years later he constructed the Home Insurance Building downtown: "The building was the first fully metal-framed building and is considered the first skyscraper". His drafting room educated a generation, as Louis Sullivan, Daniel Burnham, William Holabird and Martin Roche "performed their architectural apprenticeships on Jenney's staff". Here he provided Hibbard a sober Italianate composition, a low hipped roof on bracketed eaves. Appropriately, from 1921 its owners will grant Sullivan a complimentary office here until his death in 1924; in 1932 the residence will be demolished. Proceed to the corner, and a radically different variety of genius.

1800 Prairie, Henry Hobson Richardson's residence for John J. Glessner. Glessner recalled his architect weighing 370 pounds: "big-minded, big-bodied, big-hearted". Three weeks before his death, too debilitated to leave his bedroom, Richardson indicated the positions of the light fixtures and declared, "There, Mr. Glessner if I were to live five years longer, that is the last thing I would do on your house, my part is finished". He died on 26 April 1886; construction commenced on 1 June, and Norcross Brothers completed it for the contracted price without a single additional dollar. The neighbors were appalled, and George Pullman complained about "that thing staring me in the face". Now examine the adjacent residence.

1808 Prairie, adjacent, designed by Cobb and Frost for Osborn R. Keith. The construction notice of 1886 reads like an invoice: a three-story dwelling, 38 by 80 feet, with a granite façade, costing forty thousand dollars. It rose during the same year that Richardson's drawings next door were being realized, granite responding to granite in an architectural dialogue. When it is demolished in 1968, its north wall will be preserved to maintain the privacy of the Glessner courtyard. Two doors south stands the work of the firm that would ultimately outbuild every competitor.

1812 Prairie, George H. Wheeler's residence of 1884 by Burnham and Root: a picturesque brick row house in the Dutch manner, its façade extended upward as a tall shaped gable above a stone ground story. It will be demolished in 1968. Within a decade Burnham would direct the construction of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, the "White City". His celebrated maxim: "Make no little plans. They have no magic to stir men's blood and probably will not themselves be realized". Cross the avenue to a chateau by an architect who once planned an entire municipality.

1801 Prairie, Solon S. Beman's chateau of 1890 for the piano manufacturer William W. Kimball, executed in the French Chateauesque idiom with precipitous slate and a cylindrical tower. Beman was merely in his twenties when he "received a commission from George Pullman to design what would become the nation's first planned company town", Pullman, south of the city, an experiment in paternalistic urbanism. He additionally designed the palm room and conservatory for Pullman's own mansion farther up the avenue. Proceed south to the avenue's most renowned name and its most renowned architect.

1905 Prairie, Marshall Field's mansion, designed by Richard Morris Hunt of New York. "Hunt was the first American to be admitted to the school of architecture at the École des Beaux-Arts" in Paris, and he designed "the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty" and Biltmore, "America's largest private house". For Chicago's wealthiest citizen he constructed a broad brick and stone mansion beneath a mansard; it will conclude its existence as an aeronautical university before being demolished in 1955. One final stop, at 2100, where a young architect encountered his wife.

2100 Prairie, John B. Sherman's residence of 1874, the first of nearly a dozen Burnham and Root commissions along this avenue. Sherman administered the Union Stock Yards. During construction, his daughter Margaret married the young architect Daniel Burnham, in 1876, whereupon Sherman began advising his neighbors whom to engage. That is how a firm acquires an entire avenue: the client becomes one's father-in-law, and the father-in-law becomes one's most persuasive salesman. Burnham and Root consequently became the most prolific architects on Prairie Avenue. The residence where it originated will be demolished in 1936.

legs.story: South to the corner of Eighteenth Street.
Across Prairie Avenue to the eastern side.
South past the Coleman residence: Cobb and Frost again, in rough brown sandstone.
Onward past Twentieth Street to the final stop.

endings.text:
The walk concludes at 2100 Prairie. These seven residences constitute a sketchbook of the architects who reconstructed Chicago after the fire. Within several years Burnham will extend the lessons of this avenue to the entire metropolis through his 1909 Plan of Chicago, "the first comprehensive plan for the controlled growth of an American city".

Watch for their other façades as you explore. Every one is signed in stone.

keepsake.title: Prairie Avenue architects' list
keepsake.text: An interpretive list of six architects and the residences this walk associated with them; a modern note, not a period document.

evidence.text: Burnham & Root received nearly a dozen commissions on the street, beginning with the John Sherman house at 2100 S. Prairie.
evidence.locator: The page's history of the street, the paragraph on its architects.

evidence.text: Marshall Field Sr. residence at 1905 S. Prairie.

Richard Morris Hunt of New York and Henry Hobson Richardson of Boston were engaged to design the Marshall Field house and another; George Pullman and Marshall Field both acquired property on the street.
evidence.locator: The page's history of the street, the paragraphs on its first great houses and its architects.

evidence.text: HABS dates the building from June 1, 1886 to December 1, 1887; the house museum gives Richardson's death as April 26, 1886.
evidence.locator: HABS Part I.A.2, date of erection, data page 2; the museum biography's paragraph on his death.

evidence.text: John Glessner Residence. Built 1887; Henry Hobson Richardson, architect. Designed in the Richardsonian Romanesque style, the house is wrapped around a spacious light-filled courtyard.
The district draft reads the Hibbard house from the T-1837 register as an Italianate mansion with a rear addition: a low hip on bracketed eaves over a stone-based body, and the 1874 rear range.
William G. Hibbard Residence. Built 1869; William Le Baron Jenney, architect; Hibbard was president of a large wholesale hardware firm (read in paraphrase).
evidence.locator: The 1701 S. Prairie Avenue entry: its name line, and its description as read in paraphrase.

evidence.text: For O. R. Keith, three story dwelling, 38 by 80 feet, 1808 Prairie avenue, granite front; cost $40,000.
evidence.locator: Printed p. 28, right column near foot, paragraph beginning Architects Cobb & Frost report.

evidence.text: William W. Kimball Residence. Built 1890; Solon S. Beman, architect. Built for the prominent Chicago piano and organ manufacturer in the French Chateauesque style.

The district marker names George M. Pullman Residence, built 1870-1876, Henry S. Jaffay architect, and (read in paraphrase) a theatre of about 200 seats, a pipe organ and a bowling alley, with later additions by Solon S. Beman including a palm room and a large conservatory.
evidence.locator: The 1729 S. Prairie Avenue entry: its name line, and its description as read in paraphrase.

evidence.text: John B. Sherman Residence. Built 1874; Burnham & Root, architects. Sherman was manager of the Union Stock Yards; his daughter Margaret married the architect Daniel Burnham during construction, and Sherman often recommended the firm to his neighbors, making them the most prolific architects represented on the street.
The route, its order, its autumn afternoon, its reading times, its keepsake and its framing are modern interpretation; no historical visit, conversation or occupant on a day in 1904 is asserted.
George H. Wheeler Residence. Built 1884; Burnham & Root, architects. A picturesque brick row house in the Dutch vernacular style.
Albert Levy's photograph shows the front carried up as a tall shaped (Flemish) gable over brick upper storeys and a stone first storey.
evidence.locator: The whole print: the street front of 1812 from the walk to the gable's finial.

evidence.text: Glessner remembered Richardson weighing three hundred and seventy pounds: 'big-minded, big-bodied, big-hearted'.

Three weeks before his death, too ill to leave his bedroom, Richardson marked the places for the lighting fixtures and said: 'There, Mr. Glessner if I were to live five years longer, that is the last thing I would do on your house, my part is finished.' Glessner was convinced it was the house Richardson would most have liked to live in himself.
Norcross Brothers of Worcester, Massachusetts, built the house for the contract price, with no bill of extras.
George Pullman, across the street, complained of the Glessner house: 'I do not know what I have ever done to have that thing staring me in the face every time I go out of my door'.

Of Jenney's Home Insurance Building, 1884-1885: 'The building was the first fully metal-framed building and is considered the first skyscraper'; Louis Sullivan, Daniel Burnham, William Holabird and Martin Roche 'performed their architectural apprenticeships on Jenney's staff'.
evidence.locator: The paragraphs on the Home Insurance Building and his office.

evidence.text: In 1879 Solon S. Beman, born in 1853, 'received a commission from George Pullman to design what would become the nation's first planned company town'; he designed several buildings for the 1893 fair.

Burnham: 'Make no little plans. They have no magic to stir men's blood and probably will not themselves be realized.' He was Director of Works of the 1893 fair, the 'White City', and co-wrote the 1909 Plan of Chicago; in 1876 he married Margaret, daughter of John B. Sherman.

'Hunt was the first American to be admitted to the school of architecture at the École des Beaux-Arts'; his works include 'the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty' and Biltmore, 'America's largest private house'.
Joseph G. Coleman Residence. Built 1886; Cobb & Frost, architects. Cobb & Frost were well known for their designs in the Romanesque style, executed here in rough-faced brown sandstone.
Burnham and Edward H. Bennett's 1909 Plan of Chicago, 'the first comprehensive plan for the controlled growth of an American city'.

William G. Hibbard Residence, 1701 S. Prairie Avenue: in 1921 the house was bought by the American Terra Cotta & Ceramic Co., which gave the architect Louis Sullivan free office space there until his death in 1924. Razed 1932.
Osborn R. Keith Residence, 1808 S. Prairie Avenue: the north wall was retained during demolition in 1968 to preserve the private courtyard of the adjacent Glessner house.
George H. Wheeler Residence, 1812 S. Prairie Avenue: razed 1968.
Marshall Field Residence, 1905 S. Prairie Avenue: later converted to an aeronautical university. Razed 1955.
John B. Sherman Residence, 2100 S. Prairie Avenue: razed 1936.
